details:
**Kol Nidre**
The Aramaic declaration whose name means "all vows," which opens the evening service at the start of Yom Kippur. It annuls personal vows made to God, and it is chanted three times, each time louder. After it, the congregation recites Numbers 15:26 three times. Antisemites have historically misused it as false "proof" that Jews do not keep their promises.

**Ne'ilah**
The closing service of Yom Kippur, whose name means "locking" and which is associated with the "closing of the gates" of heaven. It is the fifth service of the day and includes the fifth Amidah. The Torah ark stays open throughout, and it ends with a long blast of the shofar (ram's horn), often followed by the song "L'Shana Haba'ah" ("Next year in Jerusalem").

**Kapparot**
A custom performed on the eve of Yom Kippur in which a live chicken, or a bag of money, is swung three times over a person's head while prayers are said. The idea is that the person's sins are symbolically transferred to it; the chicken is then slaughtered and given, or the money donated, to the poor.

**Scapegoat "for Azazel"**
In the Temple ritual described in Leviticus 16, the high priest drew lots between two goats: one was sacrificed to God, and the other, carrying the community's sins, was sent into the wilderness "for Azazel." Tradition says a crimson thread was tied to it. This ritual is the origin of the word "scapegoat."

**10th of Tishrei and the Days of Awe**
Yom Kippur falls on the 10th day of the Hebrew month of Tishrei, ten days after Rosh Hashanah (the Jewish New Year) and five days before Sukkot. It ends the ten Days of Awe (Days of Repentance) that make up the High Holy Days, and tradition says it was the day Moses came down from Mount Sinai with the second set of tablets.

**Book of Jonah**
The entire Book of Jonah is read during the afternoon (Minchah) service of Yom Kippur. Its story of the repentance of Nineveh and God's mercy fits the day's theme of atonement.

**Al Chet and Ashamnu**
The two main confessional prayers (Vidui) said on Yom Kippur, both arranged as Hebrew alphabetical acrostics. Ashamnu ("We have been guilty") is a short list of sins, and Al Chet ("For the sin...") is a longer double acrostic of 44 lines, each naming a kind of sin. They are recited aloud by the whole congregation and added to the Amidah (Shemoneh Esrei).

**Five prohibitions and the 25-hour fast**
Yom Kippur is a complete fast of about 25 hours, from before sunset to after nightfall the next day, required for adults. The five prohibitions are against eating and drinking, bathing, applying lotions or perfumes, wearing leather shoes, and sexual relations, and all work is also forbidden.

**Book of Life**
According to tradition, each person's fate for the coming year is written in the Book of Life on Rosh Hashanah and sealed on Yom Kippur. For this reason, in the day's closing prayers the word kotveinu ("inscribe us") is changed to chotmeinu ("seal us").

**Kittel**
A plain white robe that many men wear on Yom Kippur to symbolize purity and humility. It is also traditionally worn at one's wedding and used as a burial shroud.

**Kohen Gadol (High Priest)**
In Temple times, the High Priest led the Yom Kippur service and entered the Holy of Holies on this one day of the year. He pronounced the four-letter name of God (the Tetragrammaton) ten times during the service and, according to tradition, immersed himself in a ritual bath (mikveh) five times.

**Five prayer services**
Yom Kippur is the only day of the Jewish year with five services: Maariv (the evening service, which follows Kol Nidre), Shacharit (morning), Musaf (additional), Minchah (afternoon), and Ne'ilah (closing).

**"Sabbath of Sabbaths"**
A name for Yom Kippur (Shabbat Shabbaton) taken from Leviticus, reflecting that it is the holiest day of the Jewish calendar and that physical comforts are set aside entirely.

**Fast of Gedaliah and Shabbat Shuvah**
Two observances in the Days of Awe before Yom Kippur. The Fast of Gedaliah, on the day after Rosh Hashanah, mourns the assassination of Gedaliah, the Jewish governor of Judea after the Babylonian conquest. Shabbat Shuvah ("Sabbath of Return") is the Sabbath before Yom Kippur, named for a reading from the Book of Hosea that begins "Return, O Israel."

**Napoleon's March**
A melody that members of the Chabad Hasidic movement sing at the end of the Ne'ilah service. Tradition holds that Chabad's founder, Shneur Zalman of Liadi, adopted it to celebrate Napoleon's defeat.
